channel.title: Noticias del Mundo — Ciencia
channel.description: Noticias de ciencia de todas las fuentes configuradas.

item.title: AI-powered robotic laboratory paves the way for discovering next-generation heat-resistant coatings
item.description: Researchers have developed a self-driving laboratory that combines artificial intelligence and robotics to automate laboratory tasks, from accurately measuring and mixing chemical ingredients to high-temperature furnace processing and sample retrieval. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Two distinct sleep stages emerge in jumping spider, including a REM-like state
item.description: Humans and other vertebrates go through various stages of sleep, including REM (rapid eye movement) sleep characterized by rapid eye movements and muscle twitches. Can a similar sleep state be observed in spiders? Researchers from the Institute of Organismic Biology at the University of Bonn investigated this in the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata. The work is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Audit reveals suspected fabricated references across physics, chemistry, engineering and computing journals
item.description: Months after a Columbia University School of Nursing–led audit published in the Lancet reported thousands of fabricated citations in medical papers, the same research team has found the same problem in the physical sciences, engineering and computing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Protecting isn't enough—creating integrated conservation landscapes is key
item.description: New Monash University research has revealed how countries could strengthen their conservation networks by looking beyond the boundaries of national parks and protected areas—and focusing on how these areas connect. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Victorian spiritualism capitalized on the desire to transcend death to create new ways of making money
item.description: Death has never entirely stopped the living from trying to continue a conversation with their loved ones. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How shoes change our bones—and what that tells us about the evolution of walking
item.description: We tend to think of our bones as solid, unchanging support structures inside our bodies, but a recent study from the University of Chicago shows just how much they can change depending on how we use them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Biodiversity is a priority for European municipalities
item.description: As urbanization spreads worldwide, the loss and fragmentation of habitats are driving the global decline in biodiversity. At the same time, urban green spaces like parks, meadows and forests have the potential to contribute significantly to biodiversity conservation at the local and regional levels. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Interfacial intelligence: A new way to design polymer brushes
item.description: Polymer brushes are dense layers of polymer chains that can be engineered to change how a surface interacts with its surroundings. By controlling interactions with water, ions, proteins and other materials, they can reduce friction, prevent unwanted materials from sticking, improve separation and support the functionality of sensors and other devices. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fractional calculus helps 1D model mimic correlations seen in 2D phase transitions
item.description: Phase transitions are strongly constrained by spatial dimension. In conventional one-dimensional systems with short-range interactions, thermal fluctuations generally prevent continuous degrees of freedom from maintaining order over long distances. Fuente: Phys.org.

The pursuit of the impossible. Get a Special Look at Everest: The Other Side on Disney+ and Hulu now and see the film only in theaters and IMAX... Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Clouds on a lava planet challenge what astronomers expected
item.description: A rocky lava planet once thought to be too extreme to have an atmosphere appears to be wrapped in one with a reflective layer of vaporized silicate mineral clouds, the same family of compounds that make up quartz and sand. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Invites Media to Moon Landing Simulation Experience in California
item.description: Members of the media are invited to tour a new lunar landing simulator at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California's Silicon Valley on Thursday, Oct. 29, and Friday, Oct. 30. Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Jeanne Neal

item.title: Emotional content can improve how people process conversations
item.description: New in JNeurosci, Pyry Heikkinen and colleagues, from the University of Helsinki, explored how emotional meaning influences the way the human brain prioritizes information during naturally spoken conversations in a cocktail party setting. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Laser-blasted plasma shows how instabilities could heat the sun's corona
item.description: From its visible surface, the sun radiates heat at a relatively cool temperature of 5,800 Kelvin. Yet within the thin outer layer of the sun's atmosphere known as the corona, electrons can reach temperatures of millions of degrees, for reasons astronomers have yet to fully explain. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Lizard tail preserved in amber sheds light on a 100-million-year-old defense mechanism
item.description: A lizard making a dramatic escape, leaving its tail wriggling behind as it darts to safety, is an image familiar to many. Tail-shedding is one of the most widespread defenses against predators among living lizards, yet tracing the origins of this extraordinary ability has proved to be surprisingly difficult—how can we tell when this escape tactic first arose in lizards? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Solving an ancient cold case: Roman was brutally murdered
item.description: This 2,000-year-old cold case offered a wealth of information, Leiden archaeologists Carol van Driel-Murray and Mark Driessen explain. Few skeletons from the late Iron Age and early Roman era have been preserved, making this largely intact skeleton a valuable research resource. In their new book Victims of Violence from the Early Roman Fort Velsen, Van Driel-Murray and Driessen reconstruct the cause of this man's death. This interdisciplinary study combined archaeological, historical and forensic insights. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Britain's 1972 school reform may have lowered dementia diagnoses half a century later
item.description: A new study provides perhaps the strongest evidence yet that education can help mitigate long-term dementia risk. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Armored amphibian lived entirely at sea 237 million years ago, fossils suggest
item.description: Scientists report fossil evidence of the first fully marine amphibian in a study from the University of California, Davis; Peking University; and the Geological Museum of Guizhou. The amphibian is an armored, giant salamander–sized, bottom-dwelling ocean creature that the researchers named Gerrothorax maritimus. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Physicists reveal new paradigm for fiber growth in neurodegenerative diseases
item.description: Some proteins that are linked to neurodegenerative diseases can form both liquid droplets and amyloid fibers. But how are these two states connected, and where do the fibers grow? Leiden physicists Liru Feng and Louise Jawerth have discovered a counter-intuitive mechanism. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: An American startup wants to sell sunlight after dark. Who gets a say?
item.description: A U.S. startup has booked two Indian rocket launches to test a planned service no company has sold before: sunlight at night. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s X-59 Aircraft and Test Pilot
item.description: NASA test pilot Mike Lippert poses for a photo ahead of his first time flying the agency’s X-59 quiet supersonic research aircraft on Oct. 21, 2026. The X-59 has flown numerous times since its inaugural flight in November 2025; its first supersonic flight was on June 5, 2026. Lippert took off from NASA’s Armstrong Flight […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: HQ Web Team

item.title: Sediment core reveals volcanic eruption preceded ancient cold spell by about 150 years
item.description: A new study led by an international research team including scientists at the University of South Carolina challenges the idea that the ancient Laacher See volcanic eruption in western Europe triggered a significant climate-cooling period affecting central Europe and the Arctic nearly 13,000 years ago. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Stellar collisions may have been common when the universe was young
item.description: In our solar system's corner of the galaxy, stars rarely collide. It makes sense: Space is vast, and stars have room to roam. Even in most of the present-day universe, stellar collisions are rare. The James Webb Space Telescope, however, peers deep enough into space to see the universe as it was not too long after the Big Bang. Its observations have revealed extraordinarily compact stellar systems, raising the possibility that collisions between stars were once much more common. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Protein fibers, a hallmark of Alzheimer's, spotted making genetic deliveries to sperm cells
item.description: Unexpectedly, a kind of protein that is usually linked with diseases in the brain may play a vital role in semen, helping shepherd genetic material into sperm cells, scientists at Columbia's Zuckerman Institute report in the journal Molecular Cell. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Plants may switch between reproductive strategies more easily than thought
item.description: When it comes to reproduction, plants have options. Some can fertilize themselves, while others rely on pollen from genetically different plants. Many populations even contain a mixture of both strategies. But scientists have long debated whether this mixed approach is truly stable or simply a temporary stage on the way from one reproductive strategy to another. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Brain stimulation temporarily changes perception of sexualized images of women
item.description: Applying mild electrical stimulation to the brain temporarily removed a perceptual bias linked to the sexual objectification of women, in the first study of its kind. The study is published in the journal Social Neuroscience. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: RNA archiving method reveals what a cell did days ago
item.description: Information on what a cell did a few hours or days ago is generally unavailable to researchers, who can only measure the cell's current status. This is a problem if the aim is to understand how immune responses arise or why individual cancer cells survive treatment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA, USDA Sign Agreement Advancing Earth Science, Agriculture
item.description: NASA and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding expanding cooperation in Earth observation, geospatial analytics, and advanced data technologies, supporting USDA’s data modernization plan for United States agriculture. “NASA develops some of the most advanced sensing, computing, and analytical capabilities in the world, and we should put those tools […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Jennifer M. Dooren

item.title: New statewide lidar study identifies hot spots for California coastal cliff retreat
item.description: The cliffs that comprise much of California's coastline are constantly being reshaped by rain, waves and other geologic forces. The erosion of cliffs threatens critical infrastructure such as highways, railways, homes, parklands, public access points and more. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Suicide attempts, ideation spiked significantly among older U.S. adults after COVID-19 pandemic
item.description: New research from UCLA Health and UC San Diego Health found a significant spike in suicidal thoughts, planning and attempts among older U.S. adults in the years following the COVID-19 pandemic. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Both selfishness and generosity distort how we see our impact, but the selfish view is more contagious
item.description: People can sometimes make decisions that benefit them but are less advantageous for someone else. In these scenarios, they might convince themselves that their choice causes little harm to others or that an alternative would not make much of a difference. The same can happen in reverse, as people who act generously may overstate how much good the outcomes of their choices did for others. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Exercise doesn't just strengthen your heart. It rewires it
item.description: Regular exercise does more than strengthen the heart. New research reveals that it actually reshapes the nerves controlling how the heart functions, and the changes are surprisingly different on the left and right sides of the body. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Why do people overpay for used cars with mileage just below round numbers?
item.description: A recent study showed that used car dealers profit from mileage readings just under round-number thresholds. The researchers analyzed millions of transactions to determine pricing impacts of left-digit bias. Buyers often overlook minor differences in mileage, focusing instead on the first digit. This inattention allows dealers to charge more for cars that appear to be better value. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Lifestyle Desk

item.title: Mindfulness in DNP education: Cultivating resilience and leadership in advanced practice
item.description: A new study demonstrates that embedding short, asynchronous mindfulness practices into Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP) curricula effectively reduces stress, combats burnout, and builds essential leadership skills. The project evaluated student responses to brief, 1-to-5-minute mindfulness modules delivered through course learning management systems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A 2,700-year-old solar eclipse just revealed something surprising about Earth
item.description: A solar eclipse recorded more than 2,700 years ago is revealing surprising secrets about Earth's rotation and the Sun's ancient behavior. By correcting an eight-kilometer error in the location of an ancient Chinese capital, scientists were able to reconstruct a total solar eclipse that occurred in 709 BCE and obtain more accurate measurements of how fast Earth was spinning at the time. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: FAST and Arecibo point to possible dark galaxy with vast hydrogen reservoir
item.description: Astronomers have found a vast reservoir of hydrogen with something conspicuously missing: detectable starlight. The object, called AGC 322753, contains roughly 2 billion times the sun's mass in neutral hydrogen, a potential supply of material for making stars. Its radio signal suggests the gas may be rotating in a disk, yet deep astronomical images reveal no matching glow. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chinese scientists discover “D-rex,” a giant fungus with roots stretching back 65 million years
item.description: Scientists have discovered a giant new fungus in China that grows up to 20 inches tall and weighs nearly five pounds, making it the largest known of its kind. Dubbed “D-rex,” its evolutionary lineage appears to have emerged shortly after the dinosaurs went extinct, raising intriguing questions about how that ancient catastrophe may have shaped its evolution. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: New 3D thermal invisibility cloak makes objects disappear from infrared cameras
item.description: Researchers have developed a groundbreaking 3D invisibility cloak that can hide complex objects from infrared cameras while protecting them from extreme heat and cold. Instead of blocking heat, the device guides it around an object, making the object appear invisible to thermal imaging from virtually any direction. Successfully built and tested, the cloak could transform electronics cooling, thermal protection, and stealth technology. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Why China’s new estimate on Greenland ice loss speed is 55% lower than America’s
item.description: Chinese researchers have created a new model to convert satellite surface elevation data for the Greenland Ice Sheet into a detailed estimate of how much ice it has lost in recent decades. Using satellite altimetry data covering 2002 to 2023, they found that the ice sheet lost an average of about 120 gigatonnes (264.5 trillion lbs) of mass per year. This figure is considerably lower than the widely cited figure reached by Nasa, which previously estimated Greenland’s annual loss to be nearly 270... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Victoria Bela

item.title: Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
item.description: Scientists have filmed tiny magnetic vortices called skyrmions melting out of an organized lattice for the first time, revealing new ways to manipulate these unusual structures. The breakthrough could help make brain-like computers a reality, potentially enabling dramatically smaller and more energy-efficient technology. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Ice mission CRISTAL opens its wings
item.description: With its solar arrays integrated and key qualification reviews under way, Europe’s new ice-monitoring satellite, CRISTAL, is moving from assembly into the demanding testing phase that will demonstrate its readiness for the rigours of launch and life in orbit. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Archaeologists may have just found the world's oldest shipwreck
item.description: A mysterious shipwreck off Turkey’s coast may be the oldest ever discovered, dating back approximately 4,500 years to the age of the Egyptian pyramids. Although the wooden vessel has disappeared, its surviving pottery cargo reveals clues about an ancient trading network that may have connected distant Mediterranean civilizations. Researchers believe the ship may have crashed against rocks during a storm while transporting valuable goods such as oil, wine, or tree resin. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: AI detects “invisible” signs of pancreatic cancer years before diagnosis
item.description: A powerful new AI system could help doctors detect pancreatic cancer years before it becomes visible on conventional scans. The technology, called REDMOD, identified hidden warning signs an average of 475 days before diagnosis and was nearly twice as sensitive as experienced radiologists. By spotting cancer-related changes at their earliest stages, it could dramatically improve the chances of successful treatment for one of the deadliest forms of cancer. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists discover Arctic sea ice loss could be far worse than predicted
item.description: Arctic winter sea ice could disappear much faster than scientists previously expected, according to new research using climate clues from 6,000 years ago. By comparing ancient ocean sediments with modern climate models, researchers found that future winter ice coverage may be roughly one million square kilometers smaller than earlier predictions suggested. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.description: A coronial inquest into the deaths of six children in the Tasmanian jumping castle tragedy will seek to engage a planetary scientist from the US for his expert knowledge on dust devils. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.description: A modern satellite makes it possible to pursue the ancient tradition of leaf-peeping in a whole new way. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: A simple liquid can stop cavities without drilling, major study confirms
item.description: A simple liquid painted onto teeth in seconds can stop cavities without drilling, injections, or anesthesia, according to a major clinical trial involving young children. The inexpensive treatment could spare thousands of children painful dental procedures and surgery while paving the way for broader FDA-approved use. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers
item.description: Scientists have discovered a way to operate multiple silicon qubits simultaneously with remarkable accuracy, overcoming a major challenge in scaling up quantum computers. Their new technique maintained accuracy of approximately 99.9% even when all five qubits were running at once, opening the door to larger and more powerful quantum processors. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Lumina simulation brings the early universe to life on a record-breaking scale
item.description: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and Nancy Roman Space Telescope are revealing the universe's earliest chapters in detail. To help astronomers understand what they are seeing, researchers at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian have developed "Lumina," one of the largest and most detailed simulations ever created of the early universe. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03440-1 The creature’s armour cladding probably enabled it to tolerate the salty seas of the Late Triassic. Fuente: Nature.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03392-6 An eloquent analysis of the origins of human speech suggests that social cohesion, not conflict, drove our use of words. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Are salaries getting worse? Many scientists think so
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03398-0 Nature’s survey of almost 4,000 researchers shows that you’re not alone if you struggle to make ends meet or your last pay rise is a distant memory. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Nerve activity initiates autoimmune hair loss
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03258-x Understanding the triggers of autoimmunity might lead to better therapies, with hair loss among the conditions for which underpinning factors have come to light. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Jarish N. Cohen

item.title: Glimpsing archaeal microbes on the move
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03259-w How and when did cells gain the ability to crawl? Live imaging of cells from close relatives of early eukaryotes fills in a major gap in the understanding of cellular evolution. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Margaret A. Titus

item.title: Experienced teachers are quitting or reducing their hours—they're struggling to cope
item.description: Teacher shortages are affecting school systems in countries across the world. Governments have responded with initiatives to attract graduates into teaching. While much attention has focused on increasing supply, far less attention has been paid to why experienced teachers decide to leave, despite the high costs of turnover in recruitment, training and lost continuity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Researchers in the Neag School of Education are bringing a whole child screening assessment to a company that provides schools with a connected set of solutions that turn every student signal into timely, equitable, coordinated and measurable tools to track and manage supports. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Australian coral reefs face risk of collapse within 50 years without drastic action, global assessment finds
item.description: Every shallow-water coral reef ecosystem in Australia faces an extremely high risk of collapse by 2075, driven largely by projected ocean warming, according to a global assessment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Supercurrent enables the reading of quantum information without destroying it
item.description: One of the fundamental challenges of quantum computing is obtaining information from a quantum bit, or qubit. Unlike a conventional bit, which can be read repeatedly without altering its content, direct measurement of a quantum system typically causes the state to collapse before it can be determined. In other words, reading the information modifies it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Crows make decisions twice as fast as humans and monkeys
item.description: University of Tübingen researchers have shown that crows, when confronted with a visual choice, make a decision twice as fast as humans and monkeys. In the experiment, two carrion crows took just 235 milliseconds on average to identify the direction in which a dot pattern was moving and to indicate their choice—while maintaining a high degree of accuracy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Storms batter Europe, hitting power supplies, flights and phones
item.description: Storms battered northern Europe on Sunday cutting power to more than 150,000 homes, forcing the cancellation of hundreds of flights and silencing phone networks. Winds of up to 135km (84 miles) an hour were recorded in Argyll and Bute in western Scotland and fallen trees and power cables blocked roads and rail lines across the country. More than 82,000 homes in Britain, nearly 60,000 in France and at least 10,000 in Germany had power cuts inflicted by the passage of storms Boelo and Austen... Publicado también por: South China Morning Post. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Monarchs report their locations via… cellphone?
item.description: Who knew a monarch butterfly could borrow a cellphone to check in with friendly people he met on his journey? That is essentially what happens now that new technology has reduced the weight of a radio-pulse tag to less than half a gram (0.02 ounces). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Milky Way's disk grew 'upside down,' with younger stars forming in ever-thinner layers
item.description: The Milky Way is home to hundreds of billions of stars arranged in a glorious spiral pattern. But beyond the obvious spiral, our galaxy has other physical characteristics. It's divided into a galactic bulge, a galactic disk and a galactic halo. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How screening tools measure disadvantage may leave rural communities overlooked for public support
item.description: Whether a community is prioritized for public support can depend on how its needs are measured, according to new research from the University of New Hampshire. The study found significant differences in how government screening tools identify communities, particularly in rural areas where those differences could affect access to funding. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Patterns of polar vortices discovered in lead-free superlattices on silicon
item.description: A team at HZB has, for the first time, reported polar vortices in (BaTiO₃/SrTiO₃)₁₀ superlattices on silicon. These results expand the range of materials and substrates on which polar topological textures can occur and open up new options for incorporating complex ferroelectric states into silicon-based technologies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Llevamos años viendo como los viñedos españoles desaparecen sin que podamos hacer nada. Ha llegado el turno de la ingeniería genética
item.description: El 6 de agosto, entre Aldeanueva de Ebro y Alfaro, varios viñedos cortaron los primeros racimos de tempranillo blanco. Era la vendimia más temprana de la historia de la Rioja . Y no es algo extraordinario: en la DO Valencia empezaron el 3 de agosto; en Jerez, el 29 de julio ; y en Jumilla, el 27. En julio y vendimiando. Algo está cambiando en el vino europeo, lo llevamos contando desde hace años. Las grandes regiones vitivinícolas sufren estragos, mientras que hay regiones en las que nunca se han cultivado vides y el sector se dispara . España es un buen ejemplo de todo esto. según los datos… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: Protecting children from harm isn't enough—welfare systems must support healing through quality mental health care
item.description: In Quebec and across Canada, people working in child welfare do remarkable work to protect children and youth from maltreatment and to support families facing complex challenges. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A few seconds of loading time can push online learners off track
item.description: An online lesson takes an extra second to load. The wait may seem trivial, but in a study examining large learning platforms, these brief pauses were linked to unfinished assignments, lower scores and less time spent on the site. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Southern Africa's first known stenciled rock art found hiding in plain sight
item.description: Southern Africa has one of the most detailed and elaborate bodies of rock art anywhere in the world, from herds of running antelope to dancing men and humanoid beings with wings, hooves and horns. All are painted with fine brushstrokes or fingers. One thing this art lacks is stencils. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists reveal the hidden danger of missing blood pressure medication
item.description: Missing blood pressure medication could mean losing much of its protection against heart attacks and strokes, according to an analysis of more than 91,000 people. Patients who consistently took their medication experienced an 11% reduction in major cardiovascular events, while those who missed too many doses saw little or no measurable benefit. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Just two drinks a day may be far riskier than you think
item.description: A major new study reveals that drinking just two alcoholic beverages a day is associated with a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of death from alcohol-related causes, challenging the idea that moderate drinking is harmless. Researchers also found no significant overall health benefits from alcohol, with risks rising as consumption increases. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Three giant black holes discovered in a galaxy from the dawn of time
item.description: Astronomers have discovered three actively feeding black holes inside a single galaxy more than 12.5 billion light-years away, revealing a remarkable scene from the universe’s infancy. Two of the black holes are separated by just 620 light-years and are expected to eventually merge, while a third lurks farther away. One weighs an astonishing 80 million suns, and another is growing faster than conventional theories predict. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Global underground CO₂ storage hit record 43.6 million metric tons in 2024 alone
item.description: The most comprehensive record yet of carbon dioxide stored underground through geological carbon dioxide storage has been published today, revealing that 43.6 million metric tons were sequestered in 2024 alone—a new annual record—and that 421.7 million metric tons have now been stored in the past three decades. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New evidence suggests spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater
item.description: Millions of years after animals first conquered land, some took an extraordinary evolutionary U-turn and returned to the water. Using machine learning and thousands of fossil measurements, Yale scientists have uncovered surprising clues about which prehistoric creatures truly became aquatic. Their findings suggest that Spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater, while some ancient marine reptiles previously thought to be fully aquatic actually spent considerable time on land. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists discover how pancreatic cancer rewrites its DNA to escape treatment
item.description: Scientists have discovered how pancreatic cancer cells continually reshape their genetic makeup to become more aggressive, spread, and evade treatment. In laboratory experiments, blocking a key gene reversed some of these dangerous changes, revealing a potential new way to fight the deadly disease. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Sea cucumber–inspired gel could help heal damaged tissue in humans
item.description: Inspired by the ability of sea cucumbers to change the stiffness of their bodies, University of Waterloo researchers have developed a gel that could one day help repair damaged tendons and other soft tissues without leaving permanent material behind. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Low-dose aspirin linked to 70% lower dementia risk, but there's a catch
item.description: A common, inexpensive medication could hold an unexpected clue to preventing dementia. Researchers found that older adults with a specific genetic profile had a 70% lower relative risk of dementia when taking low-dose aspirin, even though previous studies found no overall protective effect. The discovery suggests that genetics could help explain why some people benefit while others do not. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Bust companies revived in ‘phoenix’ deals more likely to fail again, study finds
item.description: Exclusive: research for the Guardian shows ‘pre-pack’ deals with former management also pay far less to creditors The boss whose twice-bust business appears to be back Insolvent businesses reacquired by their previous management in “pre-pack” administrations are much more likely to fail again and tend to repay far less to creditors, research for the Guardian suggests. The study is the latest to raise questions about the practice of “ phoenixism ” – accounting’s controversial art of liquidating companies to allow directors to return with a new entity, free of debts. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - World.

item.title: The boss whose twice-bust business appears to be back despite £3m debts
item.description: Andrew Woosnam took millions from his recruitment firms before creditors, including HMRC, were left out of pocket Companies revived in ‘phoenix’ deals more likely to fail, study finds For three decades, the recruitment industry treated Andrew Woosnam well. Having learned his trade during the 1990s, he graduated to create his own firm at the turn of the millennium – which allowed him to bank millions of pounds in salary, dividends and loans and to buy assets including a grand house in Berkshire once owned by the comedians Dawn French and Lenny Henry. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - World.

item.title: This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans
item.description: For nearly a century, people in distant parts of the world have reported a bizarre experience after eating certain wild mushrooms: seeing dozens or even hundreds of tiny, colorful humans moving through the real world. Now, scientists have identified a mushroom species, Lanmaoa asiatica, responsible for these extraordinary hallucinations in China and the Philippines. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Popular cannabis sleep gummies may have a hidden dark side
item.description: A cannabis-derived ingredient commonly found in sleep gummies may be more habit-forming than previously thought, with new research showing that repeated exposure caused tolerance and withdrawal symptoms in mice. Scientists warn that CBN may carry risks similar to THC, although its long-term effects in humans remain largely unknown. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Astronomers may have discovered the first moon beyond our Solar System
item.description: Astronomers have uncovered evidence of a bizarre, potentially historic discovery: the first moon ever detected beyond our Solar System. Unlike familiar moons, this mysterious object is at least as massive as Jupiter and orbits a brown dwarf, which itself circles a star. The unusual arrangement challenges traditional definitions of planets and moons, leaving scientists unsure what to call it. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden flaw that challenges 40 years of superconductor science
item.description: A superconducting material studied for 40 years has turned out to be far more complex than scientists believed. Advanced 3D imaging revealed a hidden patchwork of crystal structures, with unusually wide boundaries that may weaken superconductivity. The discovery challenges decades of scientific assumptions and could explain why some superconductors outperform others. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Mediterranean diet may boost tiny proteins that protect the heart and brain
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising new clue to why the Mediterranean diet is so good for the heart, brain, and healthy aging. Researchers at USC found that older adults who closely followed the diet had higher levels of two tiny proteins, humanin and SHMOOSE, produced by the mitochondria, the energy-producing structures inside cells. These proteins have been linked to protection against heart disease, Alzheimer's disease, and age-related damage. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Venganza, el libro de Hitler, africanos y árabes como objetivo: el perfil del atacante en la periferia de París
item.description: De acuerdo con el diario francés ‘Le Monde’, el hombre que mató a una persona e hirió a cinco el viernes 23 de octubre le dijo a la policía que escogió a sus víctimas por el color de su piel y que su misión era vengar a los comerciantes saqueados durante los violentos disturbios que sacudieron a Francia la semana anterior. En una revisión en su residencia en Yvelines, los investigadores habrían encontrado un ejemplar de ‘Mein Kampf’, el libro escrito por Adolf Hitler. Mientras tanto, las localidades afectadas, Trappes y La Verrière, intentan procesar el terror vivido el día anterior. Fuente: France 24 - Español.

item.title: Solar storm delayed a train by 16 minutes in 1848, not 1841: How scientists solved a 155-year-old mystery
item.description: A fascinating correction has emerged from the archives concerning a train delay in Exeter. Initially reported incorrectly, researchers have clarified that the incident actually transpired on October 18, 1848. This revelation was achieved through the analysis of railway records and contemporary newspapers, alongside geomagnetic data, which pointed to a significant solar storm influencing the delay during that time. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Bell pepper colors reveal differences in sweetness, nutrients and ripeness
item.description: Raw, grilled, roasted, stuffed—there are many ways to enjoy bell peppers, also called capsicums, sweet peppers or paprika. Bell peppers originated in Central and South America and belong to the nightshade family along with tomatoes and eggplants. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tests reveal why titanium additions do not fully prevent pitting corrosion in stainless steel
item.description: Stainless steel is widely used for its corrosion resistance, but it is not invincible. In environments containing chloride ions, such as seawater, pitting corrosion can occur. These pits often start at tiny particles called inclusions embedded in the steel. Fuente: Phys.org.
